title: Choosing by purpose
summary: Five kinds of question, five chart families: bars to compare, lines for trends, pies and stacked bars for parts of a whole, histograms for spread and scatter charts for relationships.
objectives: Sort a question into comparison, trend, composition, distribution or relationship.
Pick the chart family that fits each purpose.
Insert each kind of chart in Excel and change a chart’s type.
Spot a chart whose type fights its question.

p: Almost every business question is one of five kinds. Name the kind, and the chart family follows.
“Which store sells most?” compares. “Is revenue growing?” is a trend.
“What share comes from Large stores?” is composition.
“Do bigger stores sell more?” is a relationship.
In real life: keep these five words on a sticky note above their desks. Every chart request gets sorted into one before anyone opens Excel.

terms: how a whole splits into parts
how many values fall in each range

items: which is bigger? → bar or column chart
how did it change over time? → line chart
what is the whole made of? → pie, doughnut, stacked bar
how are the values spread? → histogram, box plot
does one go up with the other? → scatter chart
write the question as a sentence and look at its verb

p: To compare amounts across categories, use **bars**. Our eyes compare lengths from a common baseline very accurately.
**Column** chart: a few categories with short names, or periods of time.
**Bar** chart: long names or many categories; the names fit on the left.
Sort the bars biggest first, unless the order means something (Lesson 2.1).
In real life: compared 14 product groups in a column chart and had to tilt every label. As a bar chart the names were readable and the ranking obvious.

terms: the zero line every bar starts from

p: To show how something changes **over time**, use a **line**. The slope shows rising and falling at a glance.
Time runs left to right, in order: April, May, June… never sorted by size.
Many periods (12 months, 52 weeks): a line. Three or four periods: columns work too.
Lesson 2.2 adds last year and other series.
In real life: plotted daily orders as a line and saw a dip every second Saturday: the market’s monthly holiday. In a table of 365 numbers nobody had spotted it.

check.q: “Has our online share of sales grown each quarter for two years?” Which purpose comes first?
check.explain: “Grown each quarter for two years” is change over time: a trend, so a line.

why.2: It’s not about how values spread.
why.3: It’s not asking whether two measures move together.

p: To show how a whole splits into parts, use a **pie or doughnut** for two to five parts, or a **stacked bar** to compare several wholes.
The parts must add up to one whole: 100% of revenue, all stores.
More than five parts, or parts of similar size? Use bars instead.
Lesson 2.3 covers when pies work and when they don’t.
In real life: showed its sales split into gold, silver and diamond as a doughnut on the shop’s monthly sheet. Three parts, one whole: it works.

p: To see how values are **spread out**, count how many fall into each range and draw touching columns: a **histogram**.
The bars touch: the ranges run on from each other.
Look for the peak, the spread, and the long tail of big stores.
Excel 2016 and later draws histograms and box plots for you (Lesson 3.1).
In real life: looked at average salary and saw nothing wrong. The histogram showed two humps: freshers and seniors, with almost no one in between.

one range of values, like ₹100–150 lakh

spec.title: Most stores take ₹100–300 lakh a year; a few take far more

p: To see whether two measures move together, plot one against the other: a **scatter chart**. Each dot is one store.
Dots rising to the right: as one goes up, so does the other.
Dots far from the crowd are worth a question: why does that store do so well?
Lesson 2.4 reads scatter charts properly, with CORREL.
In real life: plotted delivery time against distance for 5,000 orders. Most dots followed a line; a cluster sat far above it. They were all from one dark store with too few riders.

check.q: “How are our 50 stores’ revenues spread: are most of them small?” Which chart?
check.explain: How values spread is a distribution: a histogram counts stores in each revenue band.

why.0: A pie shows parts of a whole, not spread.
why.1: There’s no time in the question.
why.3: A scatter needs two measures; this has one.

demo.intro: Insert the chart that fits each question: a line for the monthly trend, a scatter for size and revenue, and fix a chart of the wrong type.

frames.say: Select **D1:E13** (months and revenue). Click **Insert › Line or Area** and choose **Line**.
Months run left to right in order. The October peak shows at once.
Select **K1:L51**: just the two columns of numbers, size and revenue. Click **Insert › Scatter**.
With the chart selected, click **+** (Chart Elements) and tick **Trendline**. (On a Mac: Chart Design › Add Chart Element.)
Someone charted the six categories as a pie? Select it and use **Chart Design › Change Chart Type › Bar**. The data stays; only the picture changes.

lab.intro: Four tables of Tulsi Mart data for FY 2025-26, each answering a different kind of question. For each task, choose the data and the chart type that fits the question. (Titles come later: here the **type** is the point.)

tasks.prompt: **“Which product category sells most?”** Chart **A1:B7** with the type that fits a comparison.
hints: Bars or columns: lengths from a common baseline.
tasks.explain: Comparison → bars. Long category names fit better on a bar chart.

expect.typeMsg: Comparing six categories: use a bar or column chart. A pie makes readers compare similar angles; a line suggests a timeline.

tasks.prompt: **“How did revenue move through the year?”** Chart the months in **D1:E13**.
tasks.explain: Trend → line, months left to right in order.

expect.typeMsg: Twelve months in order is a trend: a line chart shows the rises and dips best. (Columns suit three or four periods.)

tasks.prompt: **“What share of revenue comes from each store format?”** Chart **G1:H4**.
hints: Data G1:H4, type Pie or Doughnut.
tasks.explain: Composition with three parts → pie or doughnut.

expect.typeMsg: “Share of revenue” asks for parts of a whole. With only three parts, a pie or doughnut shows it.

tasks.prompt: **“Do bigger stores sell more?”** Chart store size against revenue: just the two columns of numbers, **K1:L51**.
tasks.explain: Relationship → scatter: size across, revenue up, one dot per store.

expect.typeMsg: Two measures and the question “does one go up with the other?”: a scatter chart.
expect.dataMsg: For a scatter chart, select just the two columns of numbers, Size and Revenue: K1:L51.

tasks.prompt: **“Are most of our stores small, with a few big ones?”** Which chart answers it?
hints: Count stores in each revenue band.
tasks.explain: A question about spread is a distribution: a histogram counts stores in each revenue band.
options: A line chart of the 50 stores
A scatter of size and revenue

why.0: Fifty slices: unreadable, and it shows shares, not spread.
why.3: That answers whether size goes with revenue, a different question.

tasks.prompt: **“Do stores with more staff sell more per day?”** Which purpose and chart?
hints: Does one go up with the other?
tasks.explain: Two measures, and whether they move together: a relationship, so a scatter.

quiz.q: “Which branch had the most complaints last quarter?” is a…
quiz.explain: Which is biggest: comparison, so bars.

quiz.q: Which chart fits “revenue for each of the last 24 months”?
quiz.explain: Change over many periods: a line.

quiz.q: What share of sales comes from three channels?
Six categories of similar size as a pie chart. What goes wrong?
options: Readers must compare similar angles, which is hard: bars are clearer
quiz.explain: Angles of similar slices are hard to compare. Use bars.

quiz.q: You chart two columns of numbers, size and revenue, as a line. What do you see?
options: A zig-zag joining stores in row order, which means nothing
quiz.explain: A line joins points in order. Stores have no order, so the line is noise. Use a scatter.

options: How values are spread across ranges
quiz.explain: It counts values in each range: a distribution.

points: Sort the question: **comparison, trend, composition, distribution or relationship**.
**Bars** compare, **lines** show trends, **pies and stacked bars** show parts, **histograms** show spread, **scatters** show relationships.
**Change Chart Type** swaps the picture without touching the data.
recap.cheat: Comparison → bar · trend → line · parts → pie or stacked bar · spread → histogram · relationship → scatter.
